rows.evidence: Q1: Materials and methods / Results (Figs. 4-11, Tables 2-3) - the authors ran their own hydroponic NFT experiment with six treatments (control, DBD plasma, nanocavitation, hybrid for 3/9/15 min), five plants per treatment, 35-day cycle, measuring fresh and dry weights, leaf number, colour, flavonoid, K and Fe.
rows.notes: The row's technology is drip irrigation, but the study is a recirculating hydroponic nutrient-film (NFT) trial, not drip irrigation; no drip system or soil-grown crop was tested, so there is no own evidence on drip and crop production (technology_mismatch). What the study does show: applying plasma-nanobubble hybrid treatment to the NFT nutrient solution for 9 min raised lettuce shoot fresh weight by 59% and shoot dry matter by 58% versus control (Results, Figs. 4-7), i.e. the ~60% figure quoted in the passage is correctly taken from the study, while plasma alone and nanobubbles alone gave no significant yield gain (Figs. 8-11); 15 min reduced yield relative to 9 min. Single site, one crop, one growing cycle, n=5 plants per treatment; means compared by Duncan's test with letter groupings only, no SD/SE or CI reported in the text; authors state generalizability limits (plant, nutrient solution, plasma method, gas flow) and the need for larger sample sizes. If a rater treated the hydroponic plasma-NB result as the claimed technology, Q2 would be yes with Q3-Q7 no, Q8 yes (Discussion limitations paragraph) and Q9 no.

notes: Full text appears complete apart from figures/tables not reproduced; reference list absent. Study is a company-funded feasibility trial of plasma-nanobubble hybrid treatment in NFT hydroponics (romaine lettuce), with no drip irrigation component.
